title: The services page an independent school actually needs
metaTitle: Services page an independent school needs
excerpt: Describe the class, lunch, and the end of the day in a parent's words. Each part needs an outcome, a boundary, and a way to visit or inquire.
alt: A hand pinning string between printed mobile screens on a wall, connecting the parts of a day the way a services page should.
caption: The string links one screen to the next. A school day should be that traceable. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should a school services page cover?
faqs.answer: The class, lunch, the end of the day, and the things you will not pretend to offer. Write an outcome, a boundary, and a next step for each. Next step means visit, or inquire if a tour is not possible yet.

faqs.question: How do you write a boundary without sounding cold?
faqs.answer: State the edge in plain hours and numbers: the day ends at a named time, and later care is either a separate list and fee or it does not exist. Learning support is a named staffing limit, not a promise that every need can be met. Clarity is the courtesy.

faqs.question: What is wrong with an icon grid of academics and pastoral care?
faqs.answer: Those labels are prospectus categories, not a Thursday. A parent cannot tell whether pastoral means a form tutor or a counselor on Tuesdays. If you cannot point to the thing on a visit, cut the tile.

markdown:
An independent school services page should list the day in the words a parent already uses. For someone deciding where a child will spend years, each part needs an outcome, a boundary, and a next step, which is to visit or inquire. A grid of vague capabilities does not help them choose.

Google's people-first guidance is a useful test. After reading, a person should feel they learned enough to do the thing they came to do. On this page the thing is to understand what the school day contains, where it stops, and how to see it in person. A tile that says "excellence" leaves them needing another search, which is the failure that guidance warns against.

## Name the day, not the department

Parents do not shop for departments. They shop for a morning, a class, lunch, the end of the day, and a person who knows their child. Write those. "Academic office," "pastoral," and "co-curricular" are how a large school files staff. A smaller school can say "the class," "lunch," "the end of the day," and "music lessons" and be clearer.

Use the words they say on the phone. The year their child would enter. The uniform. The gate. Pickup. If your families say "the junior house" and "the top floor," use those names after you have shown what they are. A renamed "learning journey" forces a translation, and translation is where doubt starts.

Four to seven items is a full page. More than that and you are reprinting the prospectus table of contents. Fewer than that and you may be hiding the thing that decides the choice, often the end of the day or learning support. Count the questions the office answers every week. Those questions are the outline.

Put the class first. Then the item parents worry about. Then the rest. Order is an argument about the day, not a tribute to every teacher who asked for a tile.

## Outcome in a parent's words

Each item should say what the child gets, in one or two sentences, with a concrete noun. The class: a group of a stated size, a teacher, a kind of work you can point at on a visit. Lunch: a room, a time, whether it is hot food or a packed lunch from home. The end of the day: the hour, who supervises, where the parent stands.

Outcome is not a promise that the child will become a certain kind of adult. "They will thrive" is a hope. "Year 4 spends the morning on a shared book, in a group of about eighteen, with the class teacher" is an outcome, and it has a boundary inside it. Specific is kinder, because it lets the wrong family opt out before the child has visited twice and started to love a place that cannot fit.

Write the sentence the way the registrar would say it on a Tuesday. Short. A little plain. If a sentence needs the word "holistic," it is not finished. Replace the adjective with the hour and the room.

If an item varies by age, say the age. After-school care that ends at 4:30 for the youngest and at 5:30 for the older children is two outcomes. Listing "wraparound" as a single glow is how a parent misses a train and blames the school for a fact you could have printed.

## The boundary

A boundary is the edge of the offer. It belongs in the same block as the outcome. You teach these ages and not others. You do not offer boarding, or you offer it only from a named year. Learning support is a named provision with a limit, not a magic promise that every need can be met. Sport is games on a field you share, not a scholarship academy with a stadium. Say the sharing.

Boundaries are how a small school stays honest about a specific child. A parent comparing three schools is often trying to avoid a mismatch: a conservatoire ambition you cannot serve, a learning need you are not staffed for, a faith practice you do not have, a bus route you do not run. The kindest page names the edge before the open morning.

Say the stair if the building has one and some classes are above it. Say that the school day ends at 3:20 and that later care is a separate list with its own fee, if that is true. A soft sentence about "flexibility for modern families" that hides a 3:20 end will be discovered. Discovery is louder than disclosure.

Do not soften a boundary into a slogan. "We meet every child where they are" is not a description of your learning support. "Two specialist teachers, working with children who already have a place, on a timetable we agree in the first term" is a boundary. If that is not what you do, do not borrow the sentence. Write the thing you do.

## One next step

Each block ends the same way: visit, or inquire if the family is not in a position to visit yet. The link can be smarter than a generic button. The learning-support block can say to mention the question in the inquiry so the right person is in the room. The end-of-day block can point at the fee line for care. The class block can name the next open morning for that age.

Do not end a block with "learn more" unless a real page sits behind it. Six "learn more" links turn the services page into a corridor. If the detail fits here, keep it here. This page is allowed to be the destination.

One action is enough. A second action, "download the prospectus," splits the decision and often hands the parent a PDF that contradicts the page. If the PDF is behind, fix the PDF or remove the button. The visit is the prospectus that can answer back.

If a program requires a separate application, such as a choir with limited places or a bus with limited seats, say so, and say what to have ready. That path is the exception. Label it so the ordinary day stays on "visit."

## Four parts of the day, written as decisions

A useful page often comes down to four blocks. You may have a fifth. You rarely need the twelfth tile from the template.

The class. Outcome: the group, the teacher relationship, the work. Boundary: size, age, what you do not offer inside the lesson. Next step: visit an open morning for that age.

Lunch and the middle of the day. Outcome: where the child eats and who is in the room. Boundary: allergies you can meet with notice, and the ones that would make the school the wrong place. Next step: visit, and mention the allergy in the inquiry if it is part of the decision.

The end of the day. Outcome: the hour and the place of pickup. Boundary: the latest supervised minute, and the fee if care extends past it. Next step: visit or inquire with the hour the family actually needs.

What you will not pretend. Outcome: a clear no, which is a service to the child's years. Boundary: no boarding, or no selective tutoring arm, or no Saturday school. Next step: if the no still leaves the family inside the offer, visit. If it does not, the page has done its job by ending the comparison cleanly.

Read the blocks to a parent who already has a child in the school. Ask which sentence is too flattering. Believe them. Current families remember the pickup line. Brand decks remember the tile.

## What a capability grid does instead

A grid of six icons with two-word labels feels like a website. It is a contents page with the contents removed. "Academic." "Pastoral." "Global." The parent cannot tell whether pastoral means a form tutor or a counselor on Tuesdays. They cannot tell whether global means a trip in year 7 or a logo on a wall.

Icons do not carry the boundary. A small pictogram of a book does not say "about eighteen in the class." The sentence does. If you love the icon, park it beside a paragraph. Do not let it replace the paragraph.

Capabilities drift into the school's hopes. "Bespoke pathways" in a school with one timetable is a boundary problem disguised as a service. Either describe the timetable, or remove the tile. Hope is not a period in the day.

Look at each cell and ask what a parent could observe on a visit. A class working. A lunch hall. A gate at 3:20. If you cannot point to it, cut the cell. The visit will be calmer because the page did not invent a school the tour cannot find.

## After the day is itemized

Someone who believes the items still wants to know who stands in the classroom and at the gate. That is the about page, and it should name people, not a founding legend. [Who actually teaches and who meets you at the door](/blog/how-an-independent-school-should-write-an-about-page) is the right next read, because a list of offerings without a responsible adult is still a prospectus performing confidence.

If you want help deciding which parts of the day deserve a block, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Bring the questions the office answered last week. Those questions are the page.
